claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 are two closely related AAA-type ATPases that assemble as hetero-hexameric structures made of alternating subunits and comprising six ADP/ATP-binding domains.
source: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 are two closely related AAA-type ATPases that assemble as hetero-hexameric structures made of alternating subunits and comprising six ADP/ATP-binding domains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to Figure 1A which shows the structure, and is consistent with established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 contain a unique domain II (DII) that protrudes from one side of the hexamer and defines two distinct faces of the ring, named ATPase-face and DII-face.
source: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 contain a unique domain II (DII) that protrudes from one side of the hexamer and defines two distinct faces of the ring, named ATPase-face and DII-face hereafter (Cheung et al., 2010; Ewens et al., 2016; Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; López-Perrote et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: DII domains comprise an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-binding (OB) fold domain (DII external) that connects to the hexameric ring by a flexible region containing a ß-stalk and a helical bundle (DII internal).
source: DII domains comprise an oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-binding (OB) fold domain (DII external) that connects to the hexameric ring by a flexible region containing a ß-stalk and a helical bundle (DII internal).
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge of the protein architecture.

claim: Each RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunit contains a nucleotide-binding pocket and the adjacent subunit in the hexamer provides the arginine finger motif required for hydrolysis.
source: Each RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunit contains a nucleotide-binding pocket and the adjacent subunit in the hexamer provides the arginine finger motif required for hydrolysis.
evidence: This describes the catalytic mechanism based on structural knowledge.

claim: Several structures of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes reveal that nucleotides are present in the complex even if they were not supplemented during purification.
source: Several structures of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes reveal that nucleotides are present in the complex even if they were not supplemented during purification (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: DHX34 was found to elute specifically only when His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 was present in pull-down experiments.
source: DHX34 was found to elute specifically only when His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 was present.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the DII-face of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring, RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 are used as scaffold platform for the interaction with other proteins, which are recruited by the DII domains.
source: In all these complexes, the DII-face of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring is used as scaffold platform for the interaction with other proteins, which are recruited by the DII domains.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from previous structural studies of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes.

claim: The C-terminal domain of RPAP3 binds at the ATPase-face of the ring through the interaction with RUVBL2 but not RUVBL1.
source: One exception is the C-terminal domain of RPAP3 that binds at the ATPase-face of the ring through the interaction with RUVBL2 but not RUVBL1 (Martino et al., 2018; Maurizy et al., 2018; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ATP binding or hydrolysis by RUVBL1 and/or RUVBL2 is essential to all the reported activities in cells.
source: ATP binding or hydrolysis by RUVBL1 and/or RUVBL2 is essential to all the reported activities in cells (Izumi et al., 2010; Rajendra et al., 2014; Venteicher et al., 2008), but the purified proteins display very weak ATPase activity in vitro (Nano et al., 2020; Gorynia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Purified RUVBL1-RUVBL2 proteins display very weak ATPase activity in vitro.
source: ATP binding or hydrolysis by RUVBL1 and/or RUVBL2 is essential to all the reported activities in cells (Izumi et al., 2010; Rajendra et al., 2014; Venteicher et al., 2008), but the purified proteins display very weak ATPase activity in vitro (Nano et al., 2020; Gorynia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase stabilizes interactions with clients and proteins involved in mTOR assembly in cells.
source: Inhibition of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase stabilizes interactions with clients and proteins involved in mTOR assembly in cells (Yenerall et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PIH1D1 in the R2TP complex and the insertion domain of Ino80 in the INO80 complex interact with the DII domains, inducing conformational changes in regions of the ATPase ring.
source: PIH1D1 in the R2TP complex and the insertion domain of Ino80 in the INO80 complex interact with the DII domains, inducing conformational changes in regions of the ATPase ring (Aramayo et al., 2018; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The interaction of PIH1D1 induces changes in a region at the N-terminus of one RUVBL2 subunit that contains two histidine residues (His25 and His27) that contribute to the interaction with the nucleotide.
source: In the R2TP complex, the interaction of PIH1D1 also induces changes in a region at the N-terminus of one RUVBL2 subunit that contains two histidine residues (His25 and His27) that contribute to the interaction with the nucleotide.
evidence: This is based on previous structural observations.

claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 associate with some components of the Fanconia Anemia pathway, and their depletion reduces the amount of the FA core complex.
source: In FA, RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 associate with some components of the pathway, and their depletion reduces the amount of the FA core complex (Rajendra et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Monoubiquitination of FANCD2 and FANCI can be rescued by siRNA-resistant versions of RUVBL1 but not by an ATPase-dead mutant.
source: Interestingly, monoubiquitination of FANCD2 and FANCI, a measure of the activation of the FA pathway, can be rescued by siRNA-resistant versions of RUVBL1 but not by an ATPase-dead mutant.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from a previous study.

claim: The assembly of the human telomerase holoenzyme requires RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 and the levels of assembled telomerase in RUVBL1-depleted cells can be rescued by the expression of the wild-type protein but not by an ATPase-deficient mutant.
source: The assembly of the human telomerase holoenzyme also requires RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 and the levels of assembled telomerase in RUVBL1-depleted cells can be rescued by the expression of the wild-type protein but not by an ATPase-deficient mutant (Venteicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An ATPase active RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex is required for phosphorylation of UPF1 by the SMG1 kinase, one of the key steps to initiate NMD.
source: An ATPase active RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex is also required for phosphorylation of UPF1 by the SMG1 kinase, one of the key steps to initiate NMD (Izumi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: NMD controls the quality of mRNAs by removing aberrant transcripts containing premature termination codons (PTCs).
source: NMD controls the quality of mRNAs by removing aberrant transcripts containing premature termination codons (PTCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NMD pathway.

claim: PTCs are generated as errors during transcription or splicing, but they also appear through germline mutations in a number of genetic disorders.
source: These are generated as errors during transcription or splicing, but they also appear through germline mutations in a number of genetic disorders (Hug et al., 2016; Kurosaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous reviews.

claim: NMD plays an important role in fine-tuning gene expression by regulating the abundance of a significant fraction of physiological transcripts.
source: NMD also plays an important role in fine-tuning gene expression by regulating the abundance of a significant fraction of physiological transcripts (Nasif et al., 2018), affecting functions such as stem cell differentiation (Lou et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The RNA helicase UPF1 and its specific kinase SMG1 bind to eukaryotic release factors eRF1 and eRF3 at ribosomes stalled at a PTC, forming the surveillance (SURF) complex.
source: First, the RNA helicase UPF1 and its specific kinase SMG1 bind to eukaryotic release factors eRF1 and eRF3 at ribosomes stalled at a PTC, forming the so-called surveillance (SURF) complex, where SMG1 is inhibited by the interaction of SMG8 and SMG9, two factors that block the access to the kinase domain (Gat et al., 2019; Melero et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the SURF complex, SMG1 is inhibited by the interaction of SMG8 and SMG9, two factors that block the access to the kinase domain.
source: First, the RNA helicase UPF1 and its specific kinase SMG1 bind to eukaryotic release factors eRF1 and eRF3 at ribosomes stalled at a PTC, forming the so-called surveillance (SURF) complex, where SMG1 is inhibited by the interaction of SMG8 and SMG9, two factors that block the access to the kinase domain (Gat et al., 2019; Melero et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Remodeling of the SURF complex by the interaction with NMD core factors UPF2 and UPF3b bound to the Exon Junction Complex (EJC) leads to the phosphorylation of UPF1 by SMG1.
source: Remodeling of the SURF complex by the interaction with NMD core factors UPF2 and UPF3b bound to the Exon Junction Complex (EJC) leads to the phosphorylation of UPF1 by SMG1, which results in the recruitment of factors that promote mRNA degradation.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of NMD initiation based on established knowledge.

claim: DHX34 is a DEAH box family RNA helicase that is required to initiate NMD.
source: A fully functional NMD response requires the contribution of several other proteins beyond the core NMD machinery, including DHX34 (DEAH box protein 34), a DEAH box family RNA helicase that is required to initiate NMD (Hug and Cáceres, 2014; Longman et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DHX34 is made of a structural core containing two canonical recombinase A (RecA)-like domains, a winged-helix domain (WH), a helical bundle (the Ratchet domain), and an OB-fold domain, followed by a short C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: DHX34 is made of a structural core containing two canonical recombinase A (RecA)-like domains, a winged-helix domain (WH), a helical bundle (the Ratchet domain), and an OB-fold domain, followed by a short C-terminal domain (CTD) (Hug and Cáceres, 2014; Melero et al., 2016).
evidence: This structural description is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DHX34 promotes UPF1 phosphorylation.
source: DHX34 promotes UPF1 phosphorylation and although the mechanism is unknown, current evidence suggests this occurring in complex with the SMG1 kinase and its substrate UPF1.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental observations.

claim: A region around the RecA domains in DHX34 binds UPF1 directly, whereas the CTD interacts with SMG1.
source: A region around the RecA domains in DHX34 binds UPF1 directly, whereas the CTD interacts with SMG1 (Hug and Cáceres, 2014; Melero et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DHX34 variants lacking the CTD domain fail to promote the degradation of a PTC-containing NMD reporter.
source: DHX34 variants lacking the CTD domain fail to promote the degradation of a PTC-containing NMD reporter (Melero et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Germline pathogenic variants of DHX34 were found in four families as specific to familiar forms of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).
source: Only recently, germline pathogenic variants of DHX34 were found in four families as specific to familiar forms of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) (Rio-Machin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The four DHX34 variants reduced the recruitment of UPF2 and UPF3b to UPF1, resulting in reduced UPF1 phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, the four variants reduced the recruitment of UPF2 and UPF3b to UPF1, resulting in reduced UPF1 phosphorylation, suggesting a link between DHX34, the NMD pathway and the etiology of some inherited forms of these myeloid malignances.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from a previous study.

claim: Knockdown of RUVBL1 or RUVBL2 reduces SMG1-mediated UPF1 phosphorylation and affects the degradation of a PTC-containing β-globin reporter.
source: Knockdown of RUVBL1 or RUVBL2 reduces SMG1-mediated UPF1 phosphorylation and affects the degradation of a PTC-containing β-globin reporter.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental observations.

claim: These defects could only be recovered with wild-type and not ATPase-dead mutant versions of RUVBL1.
source: These defects could only be recovered with wild-type and not ATPase-dead mutant versions of RUVBL1 indicating that the ATPase activity of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex is required to initiate the NMD response (Izumi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hetero-hexamers can bind directly to DHX34 in vitro and in cells in culture.
source: Here, we demonstrate that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hetero-hexamers can bind directly to DHX34 in vitro and in cells in culture.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B-E.

claim: DHX34 induces global conformational changes in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex with the RUVBL2 subunit being mostly affected.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reveals that DHX34 induces global conformational changes in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex with the RUVBL2 subunit being mostly affected.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: DHX34 destabilizes the N-termini of all RUVBL2 subunits and in consequence ATP hydrolysis activity by RUVBL2 is reduced.
source: DHX34 destabilizes the N-termini of all RUVBL2 subunits and in consequence ATP hydrolysis activity by RUVBL2 is reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by cryo-EM and biochemical data.

claim: Interacting partners can profoundly affect the structure and activity of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hetero-hexameric complexes.
source: This demonstrates that interacting partners can profoundly affect the structure and activity of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hetero-hexameric complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: DHX34 could couple the regulation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase activity to the assembly of the complexes that initiate the NMD response.
source: Our results suggest that DHX34 could couple the regulation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ATPase activity to the assembly of the complexes that initiate the NMD response.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 were co-expressed and purified as heteromeric complexes containing His-RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 in equimolar amounts.
source: For this, RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 were co-expressed and purified as heteromeric complexes containing His-RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 in equimolar amounts, and forming oligomeric complexes where two hexameric rings interact though the DII domains, as revealed by cryo-EM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and in agreement with what we described before (López-Perrote et al., 2012; Martino et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by cryo-EM data and previous studies.

claim: Of all the NMD factors tested (UPF1115-914, UPF2, UPF3b, EJC, and DHX34), only DHX34 interacted directly with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 forming a stable complex.
source: We first tested the interaction between RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes and UPF1115-914 (a truncated version lacking the flexible N- and C-terminal ends of UPF1), UPF2, UPF3b, EJC, and DHX34 by pull-down experiments using the His-tag in RUVBL1 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D). Of all these, only DHX34 interacted directly with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 forming a stable complex that has not been previously described.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: When DHX34 was pulled down from cells, both RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 were detected by western blot.
source: We then verified the in vitro results using immunoprecipitation experiments from cells. When DHX34 was pulled down from cells, both RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 were detected by western blot (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: FLAG-RUVBL1 eluted also endogenous RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, in agreement with the oligomeric nature of the complexes formed by these ATPases.
source: FLAG-RUVBL1 eluted also endogenous RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, in agreement with the oligomeric nature of the complexes formed by these ATPases.
evidence: This is an experimental observation that supports the oligomeric nature of the complex.

claim: SMG1 forms a direct complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
source: A pull-down experiment using the His-tag in RUVBL1 revealed that SMG1 forms a direct complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 and similar results were obtained in pull-down experiments using a FLAG-tag in SMG1 as bait.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pull-down experiments.

claim: The formation of a complex between RUVBL1-RUVBL2 and SMG1 excludes SMG8 and SMG9.
source: Curiously, in both types of experiments, SMG1 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2 interact but SMG8 and SMG9 were undetected in the elution, suggesting that the formation of a complex between RUVBL1-RUVBL2 and SMG1 exclude SMG8 and SMG9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: 2D averages of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 revealed hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes with putative density for DHX34 located at the DII-face of the ring.
source: 2D averages of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 revealed hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes with putative density for DHX34 located at the DII-face of the ring.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM image analysis.

claim: The interaction of DHX34 disrupts the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 dodecameric double-ring complexes.
source: The interaction of DHX34 disrupts the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 dodecameric double-ring complexes, an effect observed before in the assembly of R2TP (Martino et al., 2018; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and citations to previous studies.

claim: DHX34 attaches to the DII-face of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring flexibly.
source: An extensive 2D and 3D classification strategy of the images revealed that DHX34 attaches to the DII-face of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring flexibly and we selected the most homogenous sub-group of particles for refinement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM image processing and classification.

claim: The structure of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 was determined at an average resolution of 5.0 Å.
source: The structure of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 was determined at an average resolution of 5.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), with local resolutions up to 4.1 Å for the core RUVBL1-RUVBL2 whereas the resolution of DHX34 in the complex was around 8–10 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B — Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The local resolution for the core RUVBL1-RUVBL2 was up to 4.1 Å whereas the resolution of DHX34 in the complex was around 8–10 Å.
source: The structure of RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 was determined at an average resolution of 5.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), with local resolutions up to 4.1 Å for the core RUVBL1-RUVBL2 whereas the resolution of DHX34 in the complex was around 8–10 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B — Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM structure determination showing differential resolution.

claim: The disparity in resolution between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2 in the complex was a strong indication of the flexible attachment of DHX34 to the ATPases.
source: The disparity in resolution between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2 in the complex was a strong indication of the flexible attachment of DHX34 to the ATPases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the resolution differences observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: DHX34 binds to the internal regions of the DII domains in the hetero-hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring.
source: DHX34 binds to the internal regions of the DII domains in the hetero-hexameric RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The DII external domains (OB-folds) are mostly free and potentially accessible for interaction with other partners.
source: The DII external domains (OB-folds) are mostly free and potentially accessible for interaction with other partners (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure with speculation about functional implications.

claim: DHX34 contacts several RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunits of the complex, thus inducing global conformational changes in the structure of the ATPases.
source: DHX34 contacts several RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 subunits of the complex, thus inducing global conformational changes in the structure of the ATPases (see below).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure analysis.

claim: The average resolution of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 improved to 4.2 Å when using a mask that removed the influence of DHX34 and the protruding OB-fold domains during image processing.
source: We first analyzed the structure of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 ring using a mask that removed the influence of DHX34 and the protruding OB-fold domains during image processing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This way the average resolution of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 improved to 4.2 Å (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, Table 1) detecting the presence or absence of nucleotide in the nucleotide-binding pockets of both subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM image processing.

claim: The most striking feature in the cryo-EM map is that the N-terminal regions that contribute to nucleotide binding are visualized in RUVBL1 but not in any of the three RUVBL2 subunits.
source: The most striking feature in the cryo-EM map is that the N-terminal regions that contribute to nucleotide binding (Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019; Silva et al., 2018) are visualized in RUVBL1 but not in any of the three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a key observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: DHX34 induces changes that affect the conformation of RUVBL2 N-terminal regions in all three subunits of the complex.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that DHX34 induce changes that affect the conformation of RUVBL2 N-terminal regions in all three subunits of the complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on extensive cryo-EM classification experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3-5.

claim: The conformational changes in the N-terminus of RUVBL2 were coupled to the loss of nucleotide.
source: The conformational changes in the N-terminus of RUVBL2 were coupled to the loss of nucleotide (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits.
source: We and others have observed that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019), but whereas nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex (Figure 3D), this is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on previous observations and the current cryo-EM structure.

claim: Nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex.
source: We and others have observed that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019), but whereas nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex (Figure 3D), this is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Nucleotide is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex.
source: We and others have observed that RUVBL1-RUVBL2 co-purifies with nucleotides bound to all six subunits (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019), but whereas nucleotide remains bound to RUVBL1 in the RUVBL1-RUVBL2-DHX34 complex (Figure 3D), this is lost in all three RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The absence of density for nucleotide in RUVBL2 could not be attributed to a lack of sufficient resolution because nucleotides are clearly present in all RUVBL1 subunits in the same complex at similar resolution.
source: The absence of density for nucleotide in RUVBL2 could not be attributed to a lack of sufficient resolution because nucleotides are clearly present in all RUVBL1 subunits in the same complex at similar resolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is an argument based on comparing the resolution in different parts of the structure.

claim: DHX34 induces conformational changes in other regions of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 besides the N-termini of RUVBL2.
source: DHX34 induces conformational changes in other regions of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 besides the N-termini of RUVBL2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B — Video 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in the figures and video.

claim: These changes affect mostly to the internal regions of the DII domains and regions in the AAA-ring.
source: These changes affect mostly to the internal regions of the DII domains and regions in the AAA-ring.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: These changes do not affect key residues of the RUVBL1 nucleotide-binding pocket, which explains why ADP remains bound to RUVBL1 after the interaction with DHX34.
source: These changes do not affect key residues of the RUVBL1 nucleotide-binding pocket, which explains why ADP remains bound to RUVBL1 after the interaction with DHX34 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The structure of the nucleotide-binding pocket in RUVBL2 is not altered significantly with respect to the crystal structure of RUVBL2 bound to nucleotide.
source: The structure of the nucleotide-binding pocket in RUVBL2 is not altered significantly with respect to the crystal structure of RUVBL2 bound to nucleotide (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: It is the displacement of the N-termini of RUVBL2 that is mostly responsible for the loss of nucleotide.
source: This suggests that it is the displacement of the N-termini of RUVBL2 that is mostly responsible for the loss of nucleotide.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural observations.

claim: DHX34 affects nucleotide binding of every RUVBL2 subunit in the complex by stabilizing a conformation that displaces the N-termini of RUVBL2.
source: Together, our results reveal that DHX34 affects nucleotide binding of every RUVBL2 subunit in the complex by stabilizing a conformation that displaces the N-termini of RUVBL2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.

claim: The dimensions of the DHX34 density that we observe attached to one ring of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 can only agree with one copy of DHX34.
source: This comparison revealed that the dimensions of the DHX34 density that we observe attached to one ring of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 can only agree with one copy of DHX34, and that possibly, it is the DHX34 core domains and not the CTD that interact with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
evidence: This is based on comparison of cryo-EM volumes.

claim: Purified DHX34 can still bind RUVBL1-RUVBL2 when its flexible C-terminal domain has been deleted.
source: Accordingly, purified DHX34 can still bind RUVBL1-RUVBL2 when its flexible C-terminal domain has been deleted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The approximate mass of the volume occupied by DHX34 in the complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 is around 120 kDa.
source: In addition, we estimated that the approximate mass of the volume occupied by DHX34 in the complex with RUVBL1-RUVBL2 is around 120 kDa by using the volume programme in EMAN (Ludtke et al., 1999) (https://blake.bcm.edu/emanwiki/Volume).
evidence: This is based on computational mass estimation from the cryo-EM volume.

claim: Monomeric DHX34 and the DHX34 core domains alone have a molecular mass of 132 kDa and 111 kDa, respectively.
source: Monomeric DHX34 and the DHX34 core domains alone have a molecular mass of 132 kDa and 111 kDa, respectively.
evidence: This is based on calculation from the protein sequence.

claim: One copy DHX34 interacts with one RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hexamer forming a complex with 3:3:1 stoichiometry.
source: Together, these analyses strongly suggest that one copy DHX34 interacts with one RUVBL1-RUVBL2 hexamer forming a complex with 3:3:1 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including volume analysis and deletion experiments.

claim: All single domain deletions of DHX34 retained binding to RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 to a measurable degree.
source: We first tested a series of systematic domain deletion mutants and found that all single domain deletions retained binding to RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 to a measurable degree (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: No domain of DHX34 is sufficient and necessary on its own to mediate the interaction with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
source: As shown by the quantification in Figure 4D, no domain is sufficient and necessary on its own to mediate the interaction with RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the domain deletion experiments.

claim: Heavily N- and C- terminal truncated versions of DHX34 showed a pronounced reduction in binding to RUVBL1-RUVBL2 but they could still bind to the ATPases.
source: Heavily N- and C- terminal truncated versions of DHX34 showed a pronounced reduction in binding to RUVBL1-RUVBL2 but they could still bind to the ATPases (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Several interactions through different domains are made between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2.
source: Overall this analysis indicated that several interactions through different domains are made between DHX34 and RUVBL1-RUVBL2, which agrees with the structure of the complex that shows multiple regions of contact between DHX34 and the ATPases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the domain deletion experiments and structural data.

claim: His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2E300Q forms similar oligomers to the wild-type complex.
source: We found that His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2E300Q forms similar oligomers to the wild-type complex and, in addition, it behaves similarly to His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 when their intrinsic fluorescence was measured using a thermal denaturation assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and thermal stability data.

claim: DHX34D279A showed an ATP consumption of 24.2% compared with wild-type DHX34.
source: DHX34D279A showed an ATP consumption of 24.2% compared with wild-type (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: DHX34 is not affected by 20 min incubation time at 37°C but it is affected by 40 min.
source: We found that DHX34 is not affected by 20 min incubation time but it is by 40 min when compared to freshly purified DHX34 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on thermal stability measurements.

claim: The weak ATPase activity of His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 measured at 37°C (4.9 ± 0.8 min−1 of ATP turnover) is similar to what had been determined previously by others.
source: The weak ATPase activity of His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 that we measured at 37°C (4.9 ± 0.8 min−1 of ATP turnover) is similar to what had been determined previously by others (Gorynia et al., 2011; Lakomek et al., 2015; Matias et al., 2006; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and this value was set as 100% activity for comparison with subsequent measurements (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on ATPase activity measurements and comparison with previous studies.

claim: His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q and His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 complexes showed a significant reduction of their ATPase activity (43% and 20% ATPase activity respectively, compared to wild-type His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2).
source: His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q and His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 complexes that are mutants in only one of the two subunits showed a significant reduction of their ATPase activity as expected if not all the subunits in each oligomer are active (43% and 20% ATPase activity for His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q and His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2, respectively, compared to wild-type His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: Adding DHX34 to His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2 reduced the ATPase activity around 50% (2.5 ± 0.9 min−1).
source: Interestingly, the ATPase activity was reduced around 50% (2.5 ± 0.9 min−1) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a key finding supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: Adding DHX34 caused no effects in His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q complexes containing ATPase-dead RUVBL2 subunits.
source: Most interestingly, adding DHX34 caused no effects in His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q complexes containing ATPase-dead RUVBL2 subunits (His-RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q showed rates of 2.1 ± 0.5 and 2.0 ± 0.5 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a key finding supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: ATP hydrolysis by the His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 mutant was affected by DHX34 as in the wild-type.
source: In contrast, ATP hydrolysis by the His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 mutant was affected by DHX34 as in the wild-type (His-RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 showed rates of 1.0 ± 0.3 and 0.4 ± 0.1 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a key finding supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: DHX34 actions on the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex are mediated mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunits.
source: These results are fully in agreement with a model where DHX34 actions on the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex are mediated mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATPase activity measurements with different mutants.

claim: Removal of the His-tag from RUVBL1 had a small effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex (3.6 ± 0.7 min-).
source: Removal of the tag had a small effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex (3.6 ± 0.7 min-) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B) but addition of DHX34 caused a similar reduction of ATP hydrolysis (1.0 ± 0.5 min−1), indicating that the presence of the tag does not interfere with the action of DHX34 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: Addition of DHX34 to untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 caused a similar reduction of ATP hydrolysis (1.0 ± 0.5 min−1), indicating that the presence of the tag does not interfere with the action of DHX34.
source: Removal of the tag had a small effect on the rate of ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex (3.6 ± 0.7 min-) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B) but addition of DHX34 caused a similar reduction of ATP hydrolysis (1.0 ± 0.5 min−1), indicating that the presence of the tag does not interfere with the action of DHX34 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: DHX34 caused a reduction in the ATPase activity of untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes when RUVBL1 was mutated but not when RUVBL2 was mutated.
source: As in the case of complexes containing His-RUVBL1, DHX34 caused a reduction in the ATPase activity of untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complexes when RUVBL1 was mutated but not when RUVBL2 was mutated (Untagged RUVBL1-RUVBL2E300Q mutant consumed 2.0 ± 0.5 and 1.8 ± 0.1 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively; and untagged RUVBL1E303Q-RUVBL2 mutant showed rates of 1.1 ± 0.5 and 0.5 ± 0.2 min−1 in the absence and presence of DHX34D279A, respectively) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E–G).
evidence: This is supported by ATPase activity measurements.

claim: There is a correlation between the conformational changes induced by DHX34 and the ATP hydrolysis activity of the complex.
source: Together, these results indicate that there is a correlation between the conformational changes induced by DHX34 and the ATP hydrolysis activity of the complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined structural and biochemical data.

claim: DHX34 regulates ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunit.
source: Thus, DHX34 regulates ATP hydrolysis of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex mostly by changes in the RUVBL2 subunit.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATPase activity measurements with different mutants.

claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 directly interact with a subset of factors involved in the initiation of the NMD response.
source: Several lines of evidence show that the ATPase activity of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 regulates several cellular processes. In particular, RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 ATPase activity is needed for a fully functional NMD response and for normal levels of SMG1-mediated UPF1 phosphorylation in vivo (Izumi et al., 2010; however, how these ATPases regulate NMD was completely unknown. Here, we provide evidence that RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 directly interact with a subset of factors involved in the initiation of the NMD response and these interactions can affect greatly the conformation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 oligomers and their ATPase activity.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: These interactions can affect greatly the conformation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 oligomers and their ATPase activity.
source: Here, we provide evidence that RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 directly interact with a subset of factors involved in the initiation of the NMD response and these interactions can affect greatly the conformation of RUVBL1-RUVBL2 oligomers and their ATPase activity.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: DHX34 is an RNA helicase that binds SMG1 and UPF1 and promotes the interaction of UPF1 with UPF2 and UPF3b, UPF1 phosphorylation and the initiation of NMD.
source: DHX34 is an RNA helicase that binds SMG1 and UPF1 and promotes the interaction of UPF1 with UPF2 and UPF3b, UPF1 phosphorylation and the initiation of NMD (Hug and Cáceres, 2014; Melero et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited.

claim: Variants of DHX34 unable to facilitate UPF1 phosphorylation have been found as pathogenic versions specific to inherited forms of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).
source: Interestingly, variants of DHX34 unable to facilitate UPF1 phosphorylation have been found as pathogenic versions specific to inherited forms of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) (Rio-Machin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a recent study cited.

claim: The N-termini of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 contain two histidine residues, His25 and His27 in RUVBL2, that bind the nucleotide and contribute to maintain it within its binding pocket.
source: The N-termini of RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 contain two histidine residues, His25 and His27 in RUVBL2, that bind the nucleotide and contribute to maintain it within its binding pocket (Muñoz-Hernández et al., 2019; Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous structural studies cited.

claim: DHX34 directly affects the conformation of RUVBL2 N-termini and decreases ATP hydrolysis.
source: Here, cryo-EM reveals that the NMD factor DHX34 directly affects the conformation of RUVBL2 N-termini and decreases ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on cryo-EM and biochemical data.

claim: DHX34 distorts the N-terminal regions in all three RUVBL2 subunits that are not visible in the map, an indication that they are flexible and not attached to the hexameric ring after DHX34 binding.
source: DHX34 distorts the N-terminal regions in all three RUVBL2 subunits that are not visible in the map, an indication that they are flexible and not attached to the hexameric ring after DHX34 binding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data.

claim: These changes provide an exit route for nucleotides, which are lost in all the RUVBL2 subunits.
source: Thus, these changes provide an exit route for nucleotides, which are lost in all the RUVBL2 subunits (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural and biochemical data.

claim: DHX34 down-regulates the ATPase activity of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex in vitro.
source: We find that DHX34 down-regulates the ATPase activity of the RUVBL1-RUVBL2 complex in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ATPase activity measurements.

claim: These effects are mediated exclusively by changes in RUVBL2 and not in RUVBL1, as shown by RUVBL2 ATPase-dead mutants not being sensible to DHX34.
source: Importantly, these effects are mediated exclusively by changes in RUVBL2 and not in RUVBL1, as shown by RUVBL2 ATPase-dead mutants not being sensible to DHX34.

claim: RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 do not always share the same function in vivo.
source: Some evidence supports this model. Several reports indicate that RUVBL1 and RUVBL2 do not always share the same function in vivo (Mao and Houry, 2017).
evidence: This is based on a review cited.

source: The ATPase activity of RUVBL2 is several fold higher than RUVBL1 at least when expressed separately (Nano et al., 2020), suggesting they do not function in the same way.
evidence: This is based on a study cited.

evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the R2TP complex.
